hook: Five kinds of salmon come home every year. Here's when, and where to watch them
intro: Salmon are born in Northwest rivers, go to sea for one to five years, and come back to the very stream where they hatched to spawn and die. On the way home they stop eating, change colour, and grow hooked jaws and humped backs. Their bodies feed bears, eagles, otters and the forest itself: the nitrogen in streamside trees can be traced to salmon.

Something is running almost every month. Sockeye pour through the Ballard Locks in July, chinook and coho fill the rivers in autumn, chum crowd the small creeks from November into December, and winter steelhead follow them. In late December and January, hundreds of bald eagles gather on the upper Skagit River to feed on the spent chum.

fish.name: Chinook
fish.note: The biggest: they can top 30 pounds. Spring, summer and fall runs; spawning chinook turn dark olive to maroon.

fish.name: Sockeye
fish.note: Bright red bodies and green heads when they spawn, in rivers that run through lakes. The Adams River run in British Columbia is huge every fourth year: 2026 is one.

fish.name: Coho
fish.note: Red sides and a dark back when they spawn, and leap well; they climb into the smallest creeks after the first big autumn rains.

fish.name: Chum
fish.note: Tiger-striped in purple and green, and the males have big teeth. The easiest to watch: they spawn in small lowland creeks, often in the city.

fish.name: Pink
fish.note: The smallest and most numerous; the males grow a great hump. In Puget Sound and southern British Columbia they return only in odd-numbered years.

fish.name: Steelhead
fish.note: Washington's state fish. Unlike salmon, some survive spawning and return again. Winter runs come in from December, summer runs from May.

spots.name: Ballard Locks
spots.note: Underwater windows look into the fish ladder: sockeye peak in July, chinook in August and September, coho into October.

spots.name: Cedar River
spots.note: Sockeye spawn right through town; watch from the trail and its bridges.

spots.name: Issaquah Salmon Hatchery
spots.note: Salmon climb Issaquah Creek past the hatchery; Salmon Days fills the town in early October.

spots.name: Piper's Creek
spots.note: Chum spawn a few steps from the trail in a city park.

spots.name: Kennedy Creek Salmon Trail
spots.note: One of the densest chum runs in the state, along a short trail by the creek.

spots.name: Bonneville Dam
spots.note: Windows onto the fish ladders, where the Columbia's runs are counted fish by fish.

spots.name: Oxbow Regional Park
spots.note: Fall chinook spawn in the Sandy River's gravel bars.

spots.name: Capilano River Hatchery
spots.note: Watch fish climb the ladder through windows, in the canyon below the dam.

spots.name: Goldstream Provincial Park
spots.note: Thousands of chum, and bald eagles gathering on the river flats into the winter.

spots.name: Adams River
spots.note: In its big years (2026, 2030) one of the largest sockeye runs on Earth turns the river red in October.

care: Watch from the bank or the trail. Don't wade into the stream: the gravel holds the eggs.
Keep dogs leashed and away from carcasses: raw salmon can carry a disease that's deadly to dogs.
Leave the fish and the carcasses where they are; they feed the stream and the forest.
Fishing for salmon has its own seasons and rules, river by river: check the state or province's regulations first.
